qt: to the Commission Manuela Ripa (Verts/ALE), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), François Thiollet (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Commission is about to publish a delegated act1 to replace the current definition of ‘engineered nanomaterials’ in the current Novel Foods Regulation2. This recommendation is criticised by nongovernmental organisations in particular, but also by the French authorities and the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety (ANSES)3 and the Belgian authorities, which consider, among other pitfalls, that the 50 % threshold it sets could be detrimental to the information of the public and to the prevention of health and environmental risks. The Commission already proposed a very similar delegated act4 in 2013, which was rejected by Parliament5 in 2014. Furthermore, in May 2020, ANSES listed 37 nano substances used as food additives or ingredients in more than 900 food products6. In the upcoming revision of the Novel Foods Regulation: 1.
How many of these 37 substances will still be considered nanomaterials, and how will those that are no longer considered nanomaterials be regulated, especially in terms of authorisation?

How will consumers be informed of the presence of the latter substances (i.e. those no longer considered to be nanomaterials) in their food if these substances are not covered by the nano labelling requirement?
How will consumer health and the environment be affected?

at: (English version) to the Commission Manuela Ripa (Verts/ALE), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), François Thiollet (Verts/ALE) (25 January 2024) Subject: Information on — and risks of — nanomaterials in food The Commission is about to publish a delegated act (1) to replace the current definition of ‘engineered nanomaterials’ in the current Novel Foods Regulation (2). This recommendation is criticised by non-governmental organisations in particular, but also by the French authorities and the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety (ANSES) (3) and the Belgian authorities, which consider, among other pitfalls, that the 50% threshold it sets could be detrimental to the information of the public and to the prevention of health and environmental risks. The Commission already proposed a very similar delegated act (4) in 2013, which was rejected by Parliament (5) in 2014. Furthermore, in May 2020, ANSES listed 37 nano substances used as food additives or ingredients in more than 900 food products (6). In the upcoming revision of the Novel Foods Regulation: 1.
How many of these 37 substances will still be considered nanomaterials, and how will those that are no longer considered nanomaterials be regulated, especially in terms of authorisation?

How will consumers be informed of the presence of the latter substances (i.e. those no longer considered to be nanomaterials) in their food if these substances are not covered by the nano labelling requirement?
How will consumer health and the environment be affected?

(13 March 2024) The Commission notes that the 37 substances which are currently on the Union market and have been identified as nanomaterials by the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety (ANSES) in its 2020 report (7), are not currently defined as ‘engineered nanomaterials’ according to the definition of Regulation (EU) 2015/2283 (8). The current definition requires that materials are intentionally manufactured to consist of nanoparticles to be considered as engineered nanomaterials. The proposed revised definition of ‘engineered nanomaterials’ adapts the definition to technical and scientific progress. By removing the notion of intentionality and adding a default threshold value of 50% or more of nanoparticles in the number-based size distribution, all manufactured materials consisting of more than 50% nanoparticles will now be considered to be ‘engineered nanomaterials’. Thus, any of the 37 substances identified in the ANSES report that meet this threshold will need to be labelled as ‘engineered nanomaterials’ when continued to be placed on the market. To guarantee a high level of public health, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) assesses the risks of both ‘engineered nanomaterials’ (9) and of materials not defined as ‘engineered nanomaterials’ which may contain small particles, including particles in the nanoscale (10).
